why_this_tool: Microsoft Azure documents the strangler fig facade, the anti-corruption layer, change data capture, cutover planning and safe decommissioning as one connected set of guidance, and its emulators and containers let you rehearse all of it on a laptop.
alternatives: Debezium with Kafka Connect streams legacy database changes on open source infrastructure you run yourself; AWS Database Migration Service is a managed replication service tied to another cloud; Flyway, Liquibase and Alembic version schema changes but do no routing or integration; NGINX and Envoy give you only the facade proxy; MuleSoft is a commercial integration platform with ready-made connectors for SOAP and SFTP sources.

setup.do: Install a container runtime, the Azure CLI, the Azure Functions Core Tools and the Azurite storage emulator, so that every later step runs locally with no paid subscription.
setup.done_when: The CLI prints its version, the Functions host starts an empty project, and Azurite reports its listening ports.

setup.why: Local emulators stand in for cloud endpoints, so you can practise the whole migration at no cost. The cited section explains when emulation is a sound substitute and where it falls short.

setup.do: Start a SQL Server developer edition container with the SQL Server Agent enabled and load a small legacy schema with an orders table and a customers table.
setup.done_when: A query against the container returns rows from both legacy tables and the agent service shows as running.

setup.why: This database plays the old business-critical system that you integrate with and later retire. Change data capture relies on agent jobs, so the agent has to be running from the start.

setup.do: Create a git repository with one folder for infrastructure templates, one for the facade, one for the new service and one for the migration scripts.
setup.done_when: The repository holds the four folders and a first commit that recreates the local stack from a clean checkout.

verified.section_found: Deploy repeatable and immutable infrastructure as code

setup.why: Keeping every piece of the migration in version-controlled templates is what makes each small step repeatable and reversible later.

steps.do: Run a small legacy web app in a container and create a facade in front of it using a local API Management self-hosted gateway or a Functions proxy app, so that every client request goes through the facade.
steps.done_when: Every request to the facade address returns the same response as the legacy app, and the legacy app is no longer called directly.

source.title: Strangler Fig Pattern - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: The facade is the first move of a strangler fig migration: clients stop knowing where functionality lives. Nothing changes for users yet, which is the point.

steps.do: Create a new service for one narrow feature, such as order lookup, and configure the facade to route only that path to it while everything else still goes to the legacy app.
steps.done_when: The order lookup path is answered by the new service, all other paths by the legacy app, and switching one route setting reverses it.

source.title: Strangler Fig Pattern - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: Moving one slice at a time keeps each change small and reversible. The worked example in the cited section shows the same staged routing.

steps.do: Write an anti-corruption layer as a separate module that translates legacy column names, status codes and date formats into the new service's own model, and make it the only code that touches the legacy schema.
steps.done_when: A search of the new service finds no legacy table or column name outside the translation module, and its unit tests pass.

source.title: Anti-Corruption Layer Pattern - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: Without this layer, legacy naming and quirks leak into the new design and outlive the old system. Isolating translation in one place also gives you one place to delete after cutover.

steps.do: Enable change data capture on the legacy database and on the orders table, as the integration surface for a system that exposes no API.
steps.done_when: The database lists a capture instance for the orders table and the capture job is running.

source.title: What is change data capture (CDC)? - SQL Server | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: When the old system has no interface, its transaction log is the most reliable one: you observe changes without modifying the legacy application. The cited section explains what the capture process records.

steps.do: Query the change table after inserting, updating and deleting a few legacy orders, and load those changes through the anti-corruption layer into the new service's store.
steps.done_when: Each legacy change appears as a translated record in the new store, with the operation type preserved.

source.title: What is change data capture (CDC)? - SQL Server | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: This closes the loop from legacy write to new-model record, which is how the new system stays current while the old one remains the system of record.

steps.do: Run a parallel change on the legacy orders table: add a new column alongside the old one, create a second capture instance that includes it, backfill, switch readers, then drop the old column.
steps.done_when: Changes flow without a gap through all three phases, and the old column is gone with no failed reads in the new service.

source.title: What is change data capture (CDC)? - SQL Server | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: Expand, migrate, contract is how you evolve a live schema without breaking consumers. Capture instances do not follow schema changes automatically, so you need to see how two instances cover the transition.

steps.do: Write a cutover runbook that names the maintenance window, the freeze on legacy writes, the validation queries, the go or no-go criteria and the rollback steps.
steps.done_when: The runbook is committed, and a colleague can state from it alone when the window opens, what is checked and how to roll back.

source.title: Plan Your Workload Migration from Amazon Web Services (AWS) to Azure | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: A cutover is safe only when the window, the checks and the way back are agreed before anyone touches production. Writing the runbook exposes missing steps while they are still cheap to fix.

steps.do: Run the cutover as a rehearsal: freeze legacy writes, compare row counts and checksums between the legacy tables and the new store, then switch the remaining facade routes to the new service.
steps.done_when: The counts and checksums match, all facade routes point to the new service, and the rehearsal timings are recorded in the runbook.

source.title: Plan Your Workload Migration from Amazon Web Services (AWS) to Azure | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: Validation by reconciliation is what turns a hopeful switch into a proven one. Rehearsing locally shows how long each runbook step really takes.

steps.do: Configure the facade and the new service to emit request, error and reconciliation telemetry to a local collector, and set a retention period that covers the full observation time after cutover.
steps.done_when: A query over the collected telemetry shows zero calls to legacy routes for the whole retention period you set.

verified.section_found: Tailor storage and retention for usage patterns

steps.why: You can only declare the legacy system unused if you have kept evidence for long enough to cover monthly and quarterly jobs. Retention chosen by usage pattern keeps that evidence without storing everything forever.

steps.do: Run the decommissioning sequence on the rehearsal stack: disable the capture instances, archive the legacy data, remove the legacy routes and the anti-corruption layer, then stop the legacy containers.
steps.done_when: The stack runs and passes its tests with no legacy container, and the archive restores into a scratch database.

source.title: Architecture strategies for safe deployment practices - Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework | Microsoft Learn

steps.why: A migration is not finished until the old tool is switched off; leftover components keep costing money and attention. Doing it in a planned order keeps the last step reversible until the data is archived.

steps.do: Create a pipeline definition that rebuilds the stack from the templates, applies the schema scripts, runs the reconciliation checks and blocks promotion when any check fails.
steps.done_when: A run from a clean checkout passes end to end, and a deliberately introduced row mismatch makes the run fail at the gate.

source.title: Architecture Strategies for Designing a Workload Development Supply Chain - Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework | Microsoft Learn

verified.section_found: Implement quality gates in code promotion processes

steps.why: Customer migrations are repeated across environments, so the checks have to run the same way every time, without relying on memory. Quality gates make a failed reconciliation stop the release.

steps.do: Deploy a preproduction copy of the whole stack to a local kind cluster with the same routing rules, schema version and data volume shape as the target. A real cloud environment would need a paid subscription, so the local cluster is the substitute.
steps.done_when: The full runbook, from facade routing through cutover validation to decommissioning, completes on the cluster with every gate passing.
